Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR) has a major event coming in a few weeks: third-quarter earnings. Investors are always looking forward to these reports from Palantir because it's one of the few companies that reports on a Monday, so all eyes will be on it. Additionally, Palantir has a tremendous track record of beating expectations, and investors will be expecting another beat this quarter.

However, if it doesn't announce a beat, I would expect the stock to tumble, as that is what's currently priced in. Palantir has had an incredible run, but I think it must project continued revenue growth acceleration to maintain its run.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Palantir's growth has been impressive

Palantir's AI-powered data analytics software has become more popular over the past two decades. It started as a government-focused company, providing software to various government entities. This eventually expanded into the commercial sector, where it's seeing the fastest growth today. Still, government revenue accounts for more than half of Palantir's total revenue.

Palantir's strength lies in its ability to work within existing systems and deliver actionable insights quickly. This can work in a fully automated environment or with human intervention as the final approval before an action is performed. Palantir has become a popular way for businesses across industries to integrate AI into their existing systems, and this shows up in its financials.

During the second quarter, its U.S. commercial revenue grew at a breathtaking 149% pace, while U.S. government revenue increased 90%. Overall, Palantir's revenue rose 93% year over year to $1.94 billion. That overall figure is important to note because Palantir only guided for about $1.8 billion in Q2 revenue. That's a significant beat, but Palantir has been underguiding and overdelivering for some time.

For Q3, management expects revenue of $2.16 billion. That projects an 83% revenue growth rate, which would be a deceleration from Q2's level. However, if Palantir beats revenue expectations by a similar amount to Q2 (about $150 million), that would boost Palantir's growth rate to 96%, allowing it to continue reporting accelerating revenue growth.

It's important that Palantir does this because its valuation suggests that it needs to continue doubling each year.

title: Cathie Wood sells $16 million of surging tech stock

Cathie Wood sells $16 million of surging tech stock

Trading disclosure

Cathie Wood, head of Ark Investment Management, often takes profits when her favorite tech stocks rally.

That's what she's been doing with Palantir Technologies (PLTR), selling shares as the stock rallies ahead of its third-quarter earnings report.

Last year, the flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. So far this year, Wood's flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is up 11.05% as of Oct. 21, while the S&P 500 surged 13.32%, Yahoo Finance data shows.

Wood gained a reputation after the Ark Innovation ETF delivered a rosy 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the ETF tumbled more than 60%.

Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of Oct. 21, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -6.36%, while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 11.26% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar.

Cathie Wood remains optimistic about AI and tech revolution

Wood focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, but their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds.

Over the decade ended 2025, the Ark Innovation ETF wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to a report by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott. That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking. 

Wood defended her investment strategy after an audience member at a recent summit questioned ARK's performance compared with the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ).

Related: Cathie Wood buys $11.8 million of tumbling tech stock

"I welcome the question. Investors deserve to understand both their returns and the decisions behind them," Wood said in a post on X on Oct. 5.

She argued that the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and QQQ are built differently. QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, while ARK actively invests in companies it believes are driving disruptive innovation across industries including healthcare, financial services and transportation.

Wood has long been optimistic about AI, which she sees as a major driver of productivity, economic growth, and corporate profits in the years ahead. She has also pushed back against recent fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

In September, Wood reposted a post by David Sacks on X, saying he makes a good case that the "AI will kill humanity" headlines were orchestrated.

title: What Palantir Technologies Holders Got Right
detail:
What Palantir Technologies Holders Got Right
Bailey Pemberton
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 9:15 AM MST 4 min read
PLTR
Trade PLTR on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If Palantir Technologies sat on your watchlist instead of in your holdings, the move over the past few months may feel like a missed shot. Holding Palantir Technologies from the start of the year would have returned 20.2%, including dividends. The obvious question is what, back on 1 January 2026, could have helped you judge whether its AI-powered data platforms and government contracts were strong enough to justify those rich profit margin assumptions baked into bullish models.

A Narrative on Simply Wall St is one investor's written case for a company, with its growth, margin and multiple assumptions spelled out. Those assumptions imply an estimated Fair Value.

The move put Palantir Technologies in the middle of this trade. Scan 55 AI infrastructure stocks for other companies exposed to it.

What Palantir Investors Were Really Arguing About

The shares cost US$178 at the start of the period, which forced anyone watching Palantir Technologies to decide whether that price matched the story they believed.

On the bullish side, one narrative put Fair Value at US$440, or 148% above the start price. This view was based on Palantir reaching 32.0% revenue growth with profit margins of 18.0% over a 10-year stretch.

The more cautious view set Fair Value at US$19.79. Its author assumed 29.0% revenue growth, 14.0% profitability and a future P/E of 55.0x over 5 years as a risk aware path.

NasdaqGS:PLTR Trailing 12-Month Earnings & Revenue History as at Oct 2026
What The Evidence Did To The Palantir Technologies Debate

Palantir Technologies reported Q2 2026 revenue of US$1.94b and net income of US$1.06b, with net margin rising to 54.9%, which supported the optimistic case on growth and profitability. At the same time, repeated references to premium valuation multiples, insider selling in the hundreds of millions, and a P/E still described as expensive kept the cautious view about pricing alive. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.

The whole argument turned on whether rich margin and growth assumptions would show up in audited numbers. For any other stock, track multi quarter revenue, absolute profit and net margin against the story, then ask whether the P/E you are paying already assumes more.

What Palantir's Current Price Already Assumes

Today Palantir Technologies trades at US$202, up from US$178 from the start of the year. The selected Narrative's Fair Value sits below that quote, which frames the stock as already pricing in a strong execution story.

That Narrative leans on Palantir's AI platforms, government roots and commercial traction. Anyone paying today's price is effectively assuming high growth and wide margins persist. The question then becomes how valuation risks in the Narrative shape that bet.

Key Takeaways

Palantir stock rose 7% in the past month as five Wall Street firms, including Goldman Sachs and Barclays, set targets of $230 to $265, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 2%.

A 7% software-wide drop on Oct. 16 had no Palantir news behind it, and the stock won it all back within three sessions as software rallied, with ServiceNow and Datadog up about 11% this month too.

The Street's average target of $206 is now only about 2% above the stock, and its forward P/E sits around its five-year average of 103x.

Third-quarter results on Nov. 2 need to show U.S. commercial growth well above the 134% guide, so holding makes more sense than adding before then.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) is up 7% in the past month, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 2.2%.

Wall Street did much of the lifting, and a 7% software rout mid-month didn't stick. But the stock now sits almost right on the Street's average price target.

Most of the gain came in early October. Within about two days, Daniel Ives's Yorkville Ives & Co started coverage at Buy with a $250 target, Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to Buy at $230, and Barclays started at Buy with a $265 target, the Street's highest.

On Oct. 9, Palantir jumped 5.2% to a record close of $209.05, its first since November 2025.

On Oct. 12, Baird raised its target to $250 from $200. It pointed to how far Palantir can cut the cost of running AI (95% in one defense contractor's use case). Mizuho went to $245 from $215 on Oct. 15. Only Phillip Securities went the other way, cutting the stock to Hold.

A 7% drop that had nothing to do with Palantir

Then came Oct. 16. Palantir fell 7.2% as investors dumped software over worries about AI valuations. The software ETF IGV fell nearly 5%.

There was no Palantir news, but the drop still left the stock 11% below its record, in a correction.

And nothing in the business had changed. Q2 brought a record 220 deals worth $1 million or more, 73 of them over $10 million, and 149% growth in U.S. commercial revenue.

Knox, then a software bounce

It took three sessions to win it all back. On Oct. 19, Palantir rose 4.4% after Knox Systems announced a partnership that gives software makers a route into FedRAMP and IL5 federal clouds through Palantir's accreditations. No terms were disclosed, and the Nasdaq 100 rose nearly 2% that day.

Recently, PLTR stock was in the spotlight after the company announced a new partnership with Knox Systems for software delivery to the U.S. government. This deal will support more than 100 software and AI apps across federal environments with a focus on FedRAMP and IL5. It's worth noting that Knox, with its services, is a potential rival for Palantir. However, this deal allows the companies to cover a significant market together instead of competing. At the same time, the agreement positions Palantir for further expansion within the U.S. government ecosystem.

About Palantir Stock

Founded in 2003 and headquartered in Aventura, Florida, Palantir started building software for the intelligence community in the United States to assist in counterterrorism investigations and operations. Over the years, the company has built four principal software platforms: Gotham, Foundry, Apollo, and the Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP). These platforms provide the critical infrastructure needed to integrate customers' data and operations and run their software in virtually any environment.

While Palantir started building platforms for the government sector, it has since diversified to provide solutions to commercial customers as well. For fiscal 2025, the company generated 54% of revenue from the government segment and 46% from the commercial segment. Palantir has also diversified from a geographic perspective; for fiscal 2025, the company generated 26% of revenue from outside the United States.

title: The Best Aerospace and Defense ETFs to Buy
detail:
The Best Aerospace and Defense ETFs to Buy
Tony Dong, MSc, CETF
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 5:44 AM MST 8 min read

When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Credit: Getty Images

Global tensions are high in 2026. Russia's invasion of Ukraine continues more than four years into a grinding battle of attrition. And a large-scale attack launched against Iran by the U.S. and Israel in late February has turned into another regional war with broader and uncertain implications.

Governments around the world have been watching and acting. In June 2025, NATO, a military alliance of 32 countries including the U.S., Canada and most of Europe, held a periodic summit in The Hague. Member nations agreed to significantly boost defense spending targets from the traditional 2% of gross domestic product (GDP) to 5%.

That move was likely influenced by concerns about Russian President Vladimir Putin's expansionist ambitions, as well as pressure from President Donald Trump about America's outsized role in NATO. Now, President Trump is escalating and deescalating threats against Iran on an almost daily basis.

Together, these developments have created strong tailwinds for aerospace and defense ETFs, which attracted significant inflows in 2024 and 2025.

Price action has been more volatile this year. Indeed, some investors are using these exchange-traded funds as a hedge against geopolitical instability, while others see them as a way to benefit from a surge in global military spending. But the longer-term trend is intact.

Still, not all aerospace and defense ETFs are created equal. Before you invest, it's important to understand how each fund selects and weights its holdings, because those choices can drive very different performance outcomes.

What goes into an aerospace and defense ETF?

Aerospace and defense ETFs might sound like a narrow niche, but their holdings can be surprisingly diverse. These funds aren't just filled with companies that make fighter jets and missiles, though those are certainly represented.

The industry includes a wide mix of manufacturers, suppliers, service providers and contractors that support defense and aerospace operations in different ways.

A large portion of most defense ETFs is typically allocated to major prime contractors, which are the big companies that build complete weapons systems and platforms. The "Big 5" include:

Lockheed Martin (LMT), maker of the F-35 fighter jet, Black Hawk helicopters and HIMARS rocket systems.

RTX (RTX), formerly Raytheon, produces the Patriot missile defense system, as well as the Tomahawk cruise missile.

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has enjoyed a tremendous run over the past four years, more than doubling in value (up 110%). Much of its rise is connected to artificial intelligence (AI), with companies like Nvidia and Palantir Technologies leading the charge, up 2,320% and 1,680% over that time, respectively.

That's still happening, but the stakes are much higher now. Hyperscalers like Amazon and Alphabet are investing billions, and soon trillions, on AI, with the rewards yet to be fully seen. Both of those companies reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter, and both insist that the results will soon flow in.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

But as the market becomes more expensive, investors may not keep paying up for expectations. Take the Buffett indicator, for example, which Warren Buffett developed as an indication of how expensive the stock market is and whether or not it makes sense to buy stocks. The simple formula divides the total stock market value by the U.S. gross domestic product. Buffett explained: "If the relationship drops to 70% or 80%, buying stocks is likely to work out very well for you. If it approaches 200% as it did in 1999 and 2000, you are playing with fire." Today, it's at 297%.

That doesn't mean a market crash is imminent, but it does mean that investors should be prepared for one. If a market crash is on the way, history suggests that this is the smartest move you can make.

How to benefit from market crashes

Believe it or not, you can benefit from market crashes. That's when you can find amazing deals on top stocks, as long as you have some cash on hand to buy them. If you have to sell losing stocks to buy other ones, you'll turn paper losses into real ones. But if you put aside some cash now, you'll be ready.

Your portfolio should predominantly be made up of stocks you can hold for years or even decades. But if you own some high-growth stocks that have already appreciated in this bull market and could be at risk, now could be a good time to pocket some gains to have more cash. You might also need to rebalance your portfolio, which could involve selling even great stocks.

For example, if you invested in Nvidia a few years ago and it now represents an outsize portion of your holdings, that creates risk. You would want to sell some and be better diversified, and you might want to hold on to some of the cash to invest if there's a market crash.

title: Michael Burry Is Betting Against These 4 AI Stocks. Is He Right?
detail:
Michael Burry Is Betting Against These 4 AI Stocks. Is He Right?
Jennifer Saibil, The Motley Fool

Michael Burry became a popular voice in the investing community after he correctly predicted the 2008 mortgage crisis, shorted the market, and made a fortune. Although he closed his management fund last year, he continues to invest and share his market views in prominent social media posts.

Michael Burry, Scion Asset Management founder. Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Burry has recently been critical of the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out, and putting his money where his mouth is, he's betting against Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR), Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA), and Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU). Is he right?

1. Nvidia

Burry first disclosed Nvidia puts in the first quarter of 2025. He has compared the current AI situation to the dot-com bubble that burst in 2000 and named Nvidia the star player.

He has two main arguments. First, he says the chips aren't being depreciated properly, and their usable lifespan will be shorter than anticipated.

The second concerns Nvidia's circular financing. Nvidia has many mutually beneficial relationships with other companies, such as its agreement with CoreWeave, in which it has a large stake and which is buying Nvidia's chips.

His musings set off a firestorm between him and Nvidia, which shot back with a seven-page defense. Burry's reaction was, "I stand by my analysis. I am not claiming Nvidia is Enron. It is clearly Cisco." The difference being that Enron was a shell company used to manipulate investors, while Cisco's business simply dried up after the dot-com bust.

Is he right? The bull thesis looks strong for Nvidia. It is at the center of AI, and AI continues to develop, with unceasing demand. So far, the hyperscalers are thriving.

What I like about Nvidia is that it's not only an AI company, and that its chips are likely to fuel whatever the next chapter in technology is. However, I would heed Burry's cautions, and at this point, I wouldn't make Nvidia a central position in my portfolio.

2. Palantir

Burry first bought Palantir puts in the third quarter of 2025. Unlike the Nvidia position, he doesn't seem to have a problem with Palantir's business; he just thinks it's "wildly overvalued" and that its fundamental value is less than $50 per share.

As of this writing, Palantir stock trades at $201, which is 171 times trailing-12-month earnings and 84 times trailing-12-month sales. It is the most expensive stock in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) on a price-to-sales basis and has one of the highest P/E ratios in the index.
